Commission reporting

Sales, Excel policies, calculation and approval are separate responsibilities.

How it works

Select a system for its owner and handoff.

Systems, ownership and access
Ticketing / back office

The source owns the meaning of a sale and its payments. An extraction connector copies those records into raw warehouse tables.

Owner: Ticket operations

Access: Source-system administrator and connector owner

Excel rulebooks

These are fictional business controls stored in a SharePoint library. The workbook is an input to the calculation, not the final report.

Owner: Commission policy owner

Access: SharePoint library owner

SharePoint library

Editing the accepted workbook changes candidate input. Engineering validates a captured version before the warehouse uses it.

Logic App

The file reader needs SharePoint access; the storage writer needs Blob access. Those are separate permissions.

Owner: Integration owner

Access: SharePoint owner + Azure platform administrator

Azure Blob

Original bytes make a rejected or accepted workbook traceable. The warehouse reads a captured version, not an uncontrolled live spreadsheet.

Raw ticket tables

Preserve transaction and allocation keys before joining to policy. Raw ingestion and commission calculation are separate stages.

Validated rules

An invalid candidate remains available for diagnosis. It does not replace the previously accepted control version.

Owner: Data engineering + policy owner

Commission rows

Join transactions to the accepted policy at its declared grain. Preserve calculated amount and release/hold state separately.

Owner: Data engineering

Power BI model

The model consumes warehouse rows. Report filters and presentation must not silently become a second commission calculation.

Owner: Reporting analyst

Access: Power BI workspace administrator

Commission review

The business owner checks the payout population and exceptions before authorizing the payment handoff.

Owner: Commission business owner

Payroll handoff

This example ends at the approved handoff. Its payment-system mechanics are not simulated.

Owner: Finance / payroll

Try one example

A $600 season plan belongs to Casey at Harbor. A $240 payment arrives on August 5. The example policy deducts $30 in components from each allocation and pays 8% for plans covering six or more games.

  1. Match a rule
    6 games → 8%Plan length is the game count, not the number of seats.
  2. Allocate cash
    $240.00$360.00 of the ticket remains unpaid.
  3. Deduct components
    $210.00 commissionableThe synthetic policy deducts $30 from this allocation.
  4. Calculate
    $16.80 calculated$210.00 × 8% = $16.80.
  5. Release to report
    $16.80 payableAugust · payment date August 5.

Calculated and payable agree because this allocation is not on hold.

Rules and supporting detail

Where the number comes from

Ticket + payment
→
Warehouse rules
→
Commission rows
→
Report + review

The ticketing system provides the sale and cash received. Warehouse transformations match the product, team, period, and rate. Finance reviews the resulting rows before payroll uses an approved export.

The row a reviewer needs
QuestionEvidence
Which sale and payment?Stable ticket ID and payment allocation ID
Why this rate?Matched rule, product, game count, and effective period
Why this month?Payment date for plans; event date for group tickets in this example
Why is payable lower?Hold status and reason, beside the calculated amount

Three teams, three rulebooks

A common reporting shape can support different business policies. The rule table keeps those differences visible instead of burying them in a report formula.

Example teamRule keyIllustrative rate
HarborProduct + game count6+ games → 8%
SummitProduct + sales codeNew plan → 9%
ValleySeason + seller levelSenior seller → 10%
What this example leaves configurable

Rates, deductions, split credit, reversals, and date rules are business policy. The $30 deduction here is per allocation: a second $360 allocation would calculate $26.40, for $43.20 total. A once-per-ticket deduction would produce a different total. A real rulebook must name that grain explicitly.
